7.8.oldText: [8] 'Naturane nobis, inquit, datum dicam, an errore quodam, ut, cum ea loca videamus, in quibus memoria dignos viros acceperimus multum esse versatos, magis moveamur, quam siquando eorum ipsorum aut facta audiamus aut scriptum aliquod legamus? Velut ego nunc moveor. Venit enim mihi Plato in mentem, quera accepimus primum hic disputare solitum: cuius etiam illi hortuli propinqui non memoriam solum mihi afferunt, sed ipsum videntur in conspectu meo hic ponere. Hic Speusippus, hic Xenocrates, hic eius auditor Polemo; cuius ipsa illa sessio fuit, quam videmus. Equidem etiam curiam nostram, Hostiliam dico, non hanc novam, quae mihi minor esse videtur postquam est maior, solebam intuens, Scipionem, Catonem, Laelium, nostrum vero in primis avum cogitare. Tanta vis admonitionis est in locis; ut non sine causa ex his memoriae deducta sit disciplina.'

10.0.oldText: 58. But to hasten to a conclusion of this argument, which has already been drawn out at too great length: we have searched in vain for an idea of power or necessary connection in all the sources from which we might suppose it to be derived. It appears that, in single instances of the operation of bodies, we can never, by the utmost scrutiny, discover anything but one event following another, without being able to grasp any force or power by which the cause operates, or any connection between it and its supposed effect. The same difficulty arises in contemplating the operations of mind on body — where we observe the motion of the latter follow on the volition of the former, but are not able to observe or conceive the tie that binds motion and volition together, or the energy by which the mind produces this effect. The authority of the will over its own faculties and ideas is no more comprehensible. So that, on the whole, there does not appear in all nature one instance of connection that is conceivable to us. All events seem entirely loose and separate. One event follows another, but we can never observe any tie between them. They seem _conjoined_, but never _connected_. And since we can have no idea of anything that never appeared to our outward sense or inward sentiment, the necessary conclusion _seems_ to be that we have no idea of connection or power at all, and that these words are absolutely without meaning when used either in philosophical reasonings or in common life.

10.1.oldText: 59. But there still remains one method of avoiding this conclusion, and one source we have not yet examined. When any natural object or event is presented, it is impossible for us, by any sagacity or insight, to discover, or even guess, without experience, what event will result from it, or to carry our foresight beyond the object immediately present to memory and senses. Even after one instance or experiment in which we have observed a particular event to follow upon another, we are not entitled to form a general rule, or to predict what will happen in similar cases — it being rightly considered an unpardonable rashness to judge the whole course of nature from a single experiment, however accurate or certain. But when one particular kind of event has, in every instance, always been conjoined with another, we no longer hesitate to predict the one upon the appearance of the other, and to employ that reasoning which alone can assure us of any matter of fact or existence. We then call the one object _Cause_, the other _Effect_. We suppose that there is some connection between them — some power in the one by which it infallibly produces the other, and operates with the greatest certainty and strongest necessity.

10.2.oldText: It appears, then, that this idea of a necessary connection among events arises from a number of similar instances of the constant conjunction of these events; nor can that idea ever be suggested by any one of these instances, surveyed in all possible lights and positions. But there is nothing in a number of instances, different from every single instance which is supposed to be exactly similar — except only that, after a repetition of similar instances, the mind is carried by habit, upon the appearance of one event, to expect its usual attendant, and to believe that it will exist. This connection, therefore, which we _feel_ in the mind, this customary transition of the imagination from one object to its usual attendant, is the sentiment or impression from which we form the idea of power or necessary connection. Nothing further is involved. Consider the subject from every side; you will never find any other origin for that idea. This is the sole difference between one instance, from which we can never derive the idea of connection, and a number of similar instances by which it is suggested. The first time a man saw the communication of motion by impact, as in the collision of two billiard balls, he could not pronounce that the one event was _connected_ with the other — only that it was _conjoined_ with it. After he has observed several instances of this nature, he then pronounces them to be _connected_. What change has happened to give rise to this new idea of _connection_? Nothing but this: he now _feels_ these events to be connected in his imagination, and can readily predict the existence of one from the appearance of the other. When we say, therefore, that one object is connected with another, we mean only that they have acquired a connection in our thought, and give rise to this inference by which they become proofs of each other's existence — a conclusion that is somewhat extraordinary, but seems founded on sufficient evidence. Nor will its evidence be weakened by any general distrust of the understanding, or skeptical suspicion of every conclusion that is new and extraordinary. No conclusions can be more agreeable to skepticism than those that make discoveries about the weakness and narrow limits of human reason and capacity.

10.3.oldText: 60. And what stronger instance can be produced of the surprising ignorance and weakness of the understanding than the present one? For surely, if there is any relation among objects that it concerns us to know perfectly, it is that of cause and effect. On it are founded all our reasonings about matter of fact or existence. By it alone we attain any assurance about objects removed from the present testimony of memory and senses. The only immediate utility of all the sciences is to teach us how to control and regulate future events by their causes. Our thoughts and inquiries are therefore, at every moment, occupied with this relation. Yet so imperfect are the ideas we form of it that it is impossible to give any sound definition of cause, except one drawn from something extraneous and foreign to it. Similar objects are always conjoined with similar. Of this we have experience. In accordance with this experience, then, we may define a cause to be _an object, followed by another, and where all the objects similar to the first are followed by objects similar to the second_. Or, in other words, _where, if the first object had not been, the second would never have existed_. The appearance of a cause always conveys the mind, by a customary transition, to the idea of the effect. Of this also we have experience. We may therefore, in accordance with this experience, form another definition of cause, and call it _an object followed by another, and whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other_. But although both these definitions are drawn from circumstances foreign to the cause, we cannot remedy this inconvenience, or reach any more perfect definition that may point out that feature in the cause which gives it a connection with its effect. We have no idea of this connection, nor even any distinct notion of what it is we want to know when we attempt a conception of it. We say, for instance, that the vibration of this string is the cause of this particular sound. But what do we mean by that assertion? We either mean _that this vibration is followed by this sound, and that all similar vibrations have been followed by similar sounds_; or _that this vibration is followed by this sound, and that upon the appearance of one the mind anticipates the senses and immediately forms an idea of the other_. We may consider the relation of cause and effect in either of these two ways; but beyond these, we have no idea of it.[16]

10.4.oldText: [16] According to these explications and definitions, the idea of _power_ is just as relative as that of _cause_; and both refer to an effect, or some other event constantly conjoined with the former. When we consider the _unknown_ feature of an object by which the degree or quantity of its effect is fixed and determined, we call that its power; and accordingly, it is granted by all philosophers that the effect is the measure of the power. But if they had any idea of power as it is in itself, why could they not measure it in itself? The dispute over whether the force of a body in motion varies as its velocity, or as the square of its velocity, need not — I say — be decided by comparing its effects in equal or unequal times, but by a direct measurement and comparison.

10.5.oldText: As to the frequent use of the words Force, Power, Energy, etc., which occur everywhere in common conversation as well as in philosophy, that is no proof that we are acquainted, in any instance, with the connecting principle between cause and effect, or can ultimately account for the production of one thing by another. These words, as commonly used, have very loose meanings attached to them, and their ideas are very uncertain and confused. No animal can put external bodies in motion without the sentiment of a _nisus_ or endeavor; and every animal has a sentiment or feeling from the stroke or blow of an external object in motion. These sensations, which are merely animal, and from which we can _a priori_ draw no inference, we are apt to transfer to inanimate objects, and to suppose that they have some such feelings whenever they transfer or receive motion. As to energies that are exerted without our attaching to them any idea of communicated motion, we consider only the constant experienced conjunction of the events; and since we _feel_ a customary connection between the ideas, we transfer that feeling to the objects, as nothing is more usual than to apply to external bodies every internal sensation they cause.

10.6.oldText: 61. To summarize, then, the reasonings of this section: every idea is copied from some preceding impression or sentiment; and where we cannot find any impression, we may be certain that there is no idea. In all single instances of the operation of bodies or minds, there is nothing that produces any impression, nor consequently can suggest any idea of power or necessary connection. But when many uniform instances appear, and the same object is always followed by the same event, we then begin to entertain the notion of cause and connection. We then _feel_ a new sentiment or impression — namely, a customary connection in thought or imagination between one object and its usual attendant — and this sentiment is the original of the idea we are looking for. For since this idea arises from a number of similar instances, and not from any single instance, it must arise from that feature in which the number of instances differs from every individual instance. But this customary connection or transition of the imagination is the only feature in which they differ. In every other respect they are alike. The first instance we saw of motion communicated by the impact of two billiard balls (to return to this obvious illustration) is exactly similar to any instance that may presently occur to us, except only that we could not, at first, _infer_ one event from the other, which we can now do, after so long a course of uniform experience. I do not know whether the reader will readily grasp this reasoning. I am afraid that if I multiplied words about it, or threw it into a greater variety of lights, it would only become more obscure and intricate. In all abstract reasonings there is one point of view which, if we can happily hit upon it, will go further toward illustrating the subject than all the eloquence and copious expression in the world. This point of view we should try to reach, and reserve the flowers of rhetoric for subjects more suited to them.

11.0.oldText: 62. It might reasonably be expected, in questions that have been canvassed and disputed with great eagerness since the first origin of science and philosophy, that the meaning of all the terms, at least, should have been agreed upon by the disputants, and that our inquiries, in the course of two thousand years, should have been able to pass from words to the true and real subject of the controversy. For how easy may it seem to give exact definitions of the terms used in reasoning, and to make these definitions, rather than the mere sound of words, the object of future scrutiny and examination? But if we consider the matter more closely, we shall be apt to draw quite the opposite conclusion. From this circumstance alone — that a controversy has been long kept on foot, and still remains undecided — we may presume that there is some ambiguity in the language, and that the disputants attach different ideas to the terms used in the controversy. For since the faculties of the mind are supposed to be naturally alike in every individual (otherwise nothing could be more fruitless than to reason or dispute together), it would be impossible, if men attached the same ideas to their terms, that they could form different opinions on the same subject for so long — especially when they communicate their views, and each side turns itself in every direction in search of arguments that may give them victory over their opponents. It is true that if men attempt to discuss questions lying entirely beyond the reach of human capacity, such as those about the origin of worlds or the economy of the intellectual system or region of spirits, they may long beat the air in their fruitless contests, and never reach any determinate conclusion. But if the question concerns any subject of common life and experience, nothing, one would think, could keep the dispute so long undecided except some ambiguous expressions, which keep the opponents at a distance and hinder them from grappling with each other.

11.1.oldText: 63. This has been the case in the long-disputed question concerning liberty and necessity; and to such a remarkable degree that, if I am not much mistaken, we shall find that all mankind, both learned and ignorant, have always been of the same opinion on this subject, and that a few intelligible definitions would immediately have put an end to the whole controversy. I admit that this dispute has been so much canvassed on all sides, and has led philosophers into such a labyrinth of obscure sophistry, that it is no wonder if a sensible reader indulges his ease enough to turn a deaf ear to the proposal of such a question, from which he can expect neither instruction nor entertainment. But the state of the argument here proposed may perhaps serve to renew his attention, since it has more novelty, promises at least some resolution of the controversy, and will not much disturb his ease with any intricate or obscure reasoning.

11.2.oldText: I hope, therefore, to make it apparent that all men have always agreed both in the doctrine of necessity and in the doctrine of liberty, according to any reasonable sense that can be put on these terms, and that the whole controversy has so far turned merely on words. We shall begin by examining the doctrine of necessity.

11.3.oldText: 64. It is universally granted that matter, in all its operations, is driven by a necessary force, and that every natural effect is so precisely determined by the energy of its cause that no other effect, in such particular circumstances, could possibly have resulted from it. The degree and direction of every motion is prescribed by the laws of nature with such exactness that a living creature might as easily arise from the collision of two bodies as motion in any other degree or direction than that actually produced by it. If we are to form a sound and precise idea of _necessity_, then, we must consider where that idea comes from when we apply it to the operation of bodies.

11.4.oldText: It seems evident that if all the scenes of nature were continually shifting in such a manner that no two events bore any resemblance to each other, but every object was entirely new, with no similarity to anything previously seen, we should never in that case have attained the least idea of necessity, or of any connection among these objects. On such a supposition, we could say that one object or event has followed another — not that one was produced by the other. The relation of cause and effect would be utterly unknown to mankind. Inference and reasoning about the operations of nature would, from that moment, be at an end; and memory and senses would remain the only channels by which knowledge of any real existence could possibly reach the mind. Our idea, therefore, of necessity and causation arises entirely from the uniformity observable in the operations of nature, where similar objects are constantly conjoined together, and the mind is determined by custom to infer the one from the appearance of the other. These two circumstances form the whole of that necessity which we ascribe to matter. Beyond the constant _conjunction_ of similar objects, and the consequent _inference_ from one to the other, we have no notion of any necessity or connection.

11.5.oldText: If, then, it appears that all mankind have always granted, without doubt or hesitation, that these two circumstances take place in the voluntary actions of men, and in the operations of mind, it must follow that all mankind have always agreed in the doctrine of necessity, and have hitherto disputed merely from not understanding each other.

11.6.oldText: 65. As to the first circumstance, the constant and regular conjunction of similar events, we may perhaps satisfy ourselves with the following considerations. It is universally acknowledged that there is a great uniformity among the actions of men, in all nations and ages, and that human nature remains still the same, in its principles and operations. The same motives always produce the same actions. The same events follow from the same causes. Ambition, avarice, self-love, vanity, friendship, generosity, public spirit — these passions, mixed in various degrees and distributed through society, have been from the beginning of the world, and still are, the source of all the actions and enterprises ever observed among mankind. Would you know the sentiments, inclinations, and course of life of the Greeks and Romans? Study well the temper and actions of the French and the English: you cannot be much mistaken in transferring to the former _most_ of the observations you have made about the latter. Mankind are so much the same, in all times and places, that history informs us of nothing new or strange in this respect. Its chief use is only to discover the constant and universal principles of human nature, by showing men in all varieties of circumstances and situations, and by furnishing us with material from which we may form our observations and become acquainted with the regular springs of human action and behavior. These records of wars, intrigues, factions, and revolutions are so many collections of experiments by which the politician or moral philosopher fixes the principles of his science, in the same way as the physician or natural philosopher becomes acquainted with the nature of plants, minerals, and other external objects through the experiments he forms about them. Nor are the earth, water, and other elements examined by Aristotle and Hippocrates more like those that now lie under our observation, than the men described by Polybius and Tacitus are to those who now govern the world.

11.7.oldText: Should a traveler, returning from a far country, bring us an account of men wholly different from any with whom we were ever acquainted — men entirely free of avarice, ambition, or revenge, who knew no pleasure but friendship, generosity, and public spirit — we should immediately, from these circumstances, detect the falsehood and prove him a liar, with the same certainty as if he had stuffed his narrative with stories of centaurs and dragons, miracles and prodigies. And if we wish to explode any forgery in history, we cannot make use of a more convincing argument than to prove that the actions ascribed to any person are directly contrary to the course of nature, and that no human motives, in such circumstances, could ever lead him to such conduct. The veracity of Quintus Curtius is as much to be suspected when he describes the supernatural courage of Alexander, by which he was carried on alone to attack multitudes, as when he describes his supernatural strength and activity by which he was able to resist them. So readily and universally do we acknowledge a uniformity in human motives and actions, as well as in the operations of body.

11.8.oldText: Hence too the benefit of the experience gained by long life and a variety of business and company, in instructing us in the principles of human nature, and in regulating our future conduct as well as our speculation. By means of this guide, we ascend to the knowledge of men's inclinations and motives from their actions, expressions, and even gestures; and again descend to the interpretation of their actions from our knowledge of their motives and inclinations. The general observations stored up by a course of experience give us the clue to human nature and teach us to unravel all its intricacies. Pretexts and appearances no longer deceive us. Public declarations pass for the specious coloring of a cause. And though virtue and honor are allowed their proper weight and authority, that perfect disinterestedness so often pretended to is never expected in multitudes and parties, seldom in their leaders, and scarcely even in individuals of any rank or station. But were there no uniformity in human actions, and were every experiment of this kind we could form irregular and anomalous, it would be impossible to collect any general observations concerning mankind, and no experience, however accurately digested by reflection, would ever serve any purpose. Why is the aged farmer more skillful in his calling than the young beginner, except that there is a certain uniformity in the operation of the sun, rain, and earth on the production of vegetables, and experience teaches the old practitioner the rules by which this operation is governed and directed?

11.9.oldText: 66. We must not, however, expect that this uniformity of human actions should be carried so far that all men, in the same circumstances, will always act precisely in the same way, without allowance for the diversity of characters, prejudices, and opinions. Such a uniformity in every particular is found in no part of nature. On the contrary, by observing the variety of conduct in different men, we are enabled to form a greater variety of maxims, which still suppose a degree of uniformity and regularity.

11.10.oldText: Are the manners of men different in different ages and countries? From this we learn the great force of custom and education, which mold the human mind from infancy and shape it into a fixed and established character. Is the behavior and conduct of the one sex very unlike that of the other? It is from this that we become acquainted with the different characters nature has impressed upon the sexes, and which she preserves with constancy and regularity. Are the actions of the same person much varied in different periods of his life, from infancy to old age? This affords room for many general observations on the gradual change of our sentiments and inclinations, and the different maxims that prevail in the different ages of human creatures. Even the characters peculiar to each individual have a uniformity in their influence; otherwise our acquaintance with the persons and our observation of their conduct could never teach us their dispositions, or serve to direct our behavior toward them.

11.11.oldText: 67. I grant it possible to find some actions that seem to have no regular connection with any known motives and are exceptions to all the rules of conduct ever established for the government of men. But if we wish to know what judgment should be formed of such irregular and extraordinary actions, we may consider the sentiments commonly held about those irregular events appearing in the course of nature and the operations of external objects. Not all causes are conjoined to their usual effects with the same uniformity. An artisan handling only dead matter may be disappointed of his aim, as may the politician who directs the conduct of sensible and intelligent agents.

11.12.oldText: The common people, who take things at first appearance, attribute the uncertainty of events to such an uncertainty in the causes that the latter often fail of their usual influence, even though they meet with no obstacle in their operation. But philosophers, observing that almost every part of nature contains a vast variety of springs and principles, hidden by their minuteness or remoteness, find that it is at least possible that the contrariety of events does not proceed from any contingency in the cause, but from the hidden operation of contrary causes. This possibility is converted into certainty by further observation, when they note that, on exact scrutiny, a contrariety of effects always betrays a contrariety of causes and proceeds from their mutual opposition. A peasant can give no better reason for the stopping of any clock or watch than to say that it does not commonly go right; but an artisan easily perceives that the same force in the spring or pendulum always has the same influence on the wheels, but fails of its usual effect, perhaps because of a grain of dust that brings the whole movement to a stop. From observing several parallel instances, philosophers form the maxim that the connection between all causes and effects is equally necessary, and that its seeming uncertainty in some instances proceeds from the hidden opposition of contrary causes.

11.13.oldText: Thus, for instance, in the human body, when the usual symptoms of health or sickness disappoint our expectation, when medicines do not operate with their accustomed powers, when irregular events follow from any particular cause, the philosopher and physician are not surprised, nor are they ever tempted to deny, in general, the necessity and uniformity of those principles by which the animal economy is conducted. They know that a human body is a hugely complicated machine; that many hidden powers lurk in it, altogether beyond our comprehension; that to us it must often appear very uncertain in its operations; and that therefore the irregular events that outwardly show themselves can be no proof that the laws of nature are not observed with the greatest regularity in its internal operations and government.

11.14.oldText: 68. The philosopher, if he is consistent, must apply the same reasoning to the actions and volitions of intelligent agents. The most irregular and unexpected decisions of men can frequently be accounted for by those who know every particular circumstance of their character and situation. A person of an obliging disposition gives a peevish answer — but he has a toothache, or has not dined. A stupid fellow shows an unusual readiness in his bearing — but he has met with a sudden piece of good fortune. Even when an action, as sometimes happens, cannot be specifically accounted for, either by the person himself or by others, we know in general that the characters of men are, to a certain degree, inconstant and irregular. This is, in a way, the constant character of human nature, though it applies in a more particular way to some persons who have no fixed rule for their conduct but proceed in a continued course of caprice and inconstancy. The internal principles and motives may operate uniformly, despite these seeming irregularities, in the same way as the winds, rain, clouds, and other variations of the weather are supposed to be governed by steady principles, though not easily discoverable by human sagacity and inquiry.

11.15.oldText: 69. Thus it appears not only that the conjunction between motives and voluntary actions is as regular and uniform as that between cause and effect in any part of nature, but also that this regular conjunction has been universally acknowledged among mankind and has never been the subject of dispute, either in philosophy or in common life. Now, since it is from past experience that we draw all inferences about the future, and since we conclude that objects will always be conjoined together which we find to have always been conjoined, it may seem superfluous to prove that this experienced uniformity in human actions is a source from which we draw _inferences_ about them. But to throw the argument into a greater variety of lights, we shall also insist, though briefly, on this latter topic.

11.16.oldText: The mutual dependence of men is so great in all societies that scarcely any human action is entirely complete in itself, or performed without some reference to the actions of others, which are needed to make it fully answer to the intention of the agent. The poorest artisan, who works alone, expects at least the protection of the magistrate to ensure his enjoyment of the fruits of his labor. He also expects that when he carries his goods to market and offers them at a reasonable price, he will find buyers, and will be able, with the money he gains, to engage others to supply him with the commodities required for his subsistence. As men extend their dealings and make their interactions with others more complicated, they always include in their plans for life a greater variety of voluntary actions, which they expect, from the proper motives, to cooperate with their own. In all these conclusions they take their measures from past experience, in the same way as in their reasonings about external objects, and firmly believe that men, as well as all the elements, will continue in their operations the same as they have always found them. A manufacturer counts on the labor of his servants for the execution of any work as much as on the tools he uses, and would be equally surprised were his expectations disappointed. In short, this experimental inference and reasoning about the actions of others enters so much into human life that no man, while awake, is ever a moment without employing it. Have we not reason, therefore, to affirm that all mankind have always agreed in the doctrine of necessity, according to the foregoing definition and explication of it?

11.17.oldText: 70. Nor have philosophers ever held a different opinion from the common people on this particular point. For — not to mention that almost every action of their life supposes that opinion — there are few of the speculative parts of learning to which it is not essential. What would become of _history_, if we did not have a dependence on the truthfulness of the historian, in accordance with the experience we have had of mankind? How could _politics_ be a science, if laws and forms of government had not a uniform influence on society? Where would be the foundation of _morals_, if particular characters had no certain or determinate power to produce particular sentiments, and if these sentiments had no constant operation on actions? And with what pretense could we employ our _criticism_ on any poet or polite author, if we could not pronounce the conduct and sentiments of his characters either natural or unnatural to such characters in such circumstances? It seems almost impossible, then, to engage in either science or action of any kind without acknowledging the doctrine of necessity, and this _inference_ from motive to voluntary action, from character to conduct.

11.18.oldText: And indeed, when we consider how aptly _natural_ and _moral_ evidence link together and form only one chain of argument, we shall have no hesitation in granting that they are of the same nature, and derive from the same principles. A prisoner who has neither money nor influence discovers the impossibility of his escape as much when he considers the obstinacy of the jailer as when he considers the walls and bars surrounding him; and in all attempts at freedom he chooses rather to work on the stone and iron of the one than on the inflexible nature of the other. The same prisoner, when led to the scaffold, foresees his death as certainly from the constancy and fidelity of his guards as from the operation of the axe or wheel. His mind runs along a certain train of ideas: the refusal of the soldiers to consent to his escape; the action of the executioner; the separation of head and body; bleeding, convulsive motions, and death. Here is a connected chain of natural causes and voluntary actions; but the mind feels no difference between them in passing from one link to another, nor is it less certain of the future event than if it were connected with the objects present to memory or senses by a train of causes cemented together by what we are pleased to call a _physical_ necessity. The same experienced union has the same effect on the mind, whether the united objects are motives, volition, and actions, or figure and motion. We may change the name of things, but their nature and their operation on the understanding never change.

11.19.oldText: Were a man, whom I know to be honest and rich, and with whom I live in close friendship, to come into my house, where I am surrounded by my servants, I rest assured that he is not going to stab me before he leaves, in order to rob me of my silver inkstand; and I no more suspect this event than the falling of the house itself, which is new and solidly built and founded. _But he may have been seized with a sudden and unknown frenzy._ — So may a sudden earthquake arise, and shake and tumble my house about my ears. I shall therefore change the supposition. I shall say that I know with certainty that he is not going to put his hand into the fire and hold it there until it is consumed; and this event I think I can predict with the same assurance as that, if he throws himself out the window and meets no obstruction, he will not remain a moment suspended in the air. No suspicion of an unknown frenzy can give the slightest possibility to the former event, which is so contrary to all the known principles of human nature. A man who at noon leaves his purse full of gold on the pavement at Charing Cross may as well expect that it will fly away like a feather as that he will find it untouched an hour later. More than half of human reasonings contain inferences of a similar nature, attended by greater or lesser degrees of certainty in proportion to our experience of the usual conduct of mankind in such particular situations.

11.20.oldText: 71. I have often considered what could possibly be the reason why all mankind, though they have always, without hesitation, acknowledged the doctrine of necessity in their whole practice and reasoning, have yet shown such reluctance to acknowledge it in words, and have rather shown a tendency, in all ages, to profess the contrary opinion. The matter, I think, may be accounted for as follows. If we examine the operations of body, and the production of effects from their causes, we shall find that all our faculties can never carry us further in our knowledge of this relation than barely to observe that particular objects are _constantly conjoined_ together, and that the mind is carried, by a _customary transition_, from the appearance of one to the belief in the other. But although this conclusion regarding human ignorance is the result of the strictest scrutiny of this subject, men still entertain a strong propensity to believe that they penetrate further into the powers of nature, and perceive something like a necessary connection between cause and effect. When, on the other hand, they turn their reflections toward the operations of their own minds, and _feel_ no such connection of the motive and the action, they are thence apt to suppose that there is a difference between the effects which result from material force and those which arise from thought and intelligence. But once we are convinced that we know nothing further of causation of any kind than merely the _constant conjunction_ of objects, and the consequent _inference_ of the mind from one to another, and find that these two circumstances are universally allowed to take place in voluntary actions, we may more easily be led to acknowledge the same necessity common to all causes. And although this reasoning may contradict the systems of many philosophers in ascribing necessity to the determinations of the will, we shall find, on reflection, that they dissent from it only in words, not in their real sentiment. Necessity, in the sense in which it is here taken, has never yet been rejected, nor can ever, I think, be rejected by any philosopher. It may only perhaps be claimed that the mind can perceive, in the operations of matter, some further connection between cause and effect — a connection that has no place in the voluntary actions of intelligent beings. Whether it is so or not can only appear on examination; and it is incumbent on these philosophers to make good their assertion by defining or describing that necessity, and pointing it out to us in the operations of material causes.

11.21.oldText: 72. It would seem, indeed, that men begin at the wrong end of this question concerning liberty and necessity when they enter upon it by examining the faculties of the soul, the influence of the understanding, and the operations of the will. Let them first discuss a simpler question, namely the operations of body and of brute unintelligent matter, and try whether they can there form any idea of causation and necessity except that of a constant conjunction of objects and subsequent inference of the mind from one to another. If these circumstances form, in reality, the whole of that necessity we conceive in matter, and if these circumstances are also universally acknowledged to take place in the operations of the mind, the dispute is at an end — or at least must be admitted, from then on, to be merely verbal. But as long as we will rashly suppose that we have some further idea of necessity and causation in the operations of external objects, while at the same time we can find nothing further in the voluntary actions of the mind, there is no possibility of bringing the question to any determinate issue while we proceed on so mistaken a supposition. The only way to undeceive us is to climb higher: to examine the narrow extent of science when applied to material causes, and to convince ourselves that all we know of them is the constant conjunction and inference mentioned above. We may perhaps find that it is with difficulty we are induced to fix such narrow limits to human understanding; but we can then find no difficulty when we come to apply this doctrine to the actions of the will. For since it is evident that these have a regular conjunction with motives, circumstances, and characters, and since we always draw inferences from one to the other, we must be obliged to acknowledge in words that necessity which we have already avowed in every deliberation of our lives, and in every step of our conduct and behavior.[17]

11.22.oldText: [17] The prevalence of the doctrine of liberty may be accounted for by another cause, namely a false sensation, or seeming experience, that we have, or may have, of liberty or indifference in many of our actions. The necessity of any action, whether of matter or of mind, is not, strictly speaking, a quality in the agent, but in any thinking or intelligent being who may consider the action; and it consists chiefly in the determination of his thoughts to infer the existence of that action from some preceding objects, just as liberty, when opposed to necessity, is nothing but the absence of that determination, and a certain looseness or indifference that we feel in passing, or not passing, from the idea of one object to that of any succeeding one. Now we may observe that, although in _reflecting_ on human actions we seldom feel such looseness or indifference, but are commonly able to infer them with considerable certainty from their motives and from the dispositions of the agent, it frequently happens that, in _performing_ the actions themselves, we are aware of something like it. And since all resembling objects are readily taken for each other, this has been used as a demonstrative and even intuitive proof of human liberty. We feel that our actions are subject to our will on most occasions, and imagine we feel that the will itself is subject to nothing, because when, by a denial of it, we are provoked to test the matter, we feel that it moves easily every way, and produces an image of itself (or a _Velleity_, as it is called in the schools) even on the side on which it did not finally settle. This image, or faint motion, we persuade ourselves, could at that time have been completed into the thing itself, because, should that be denied, we find, on a second trial, that at present it can be. We do not consider that the fanciful desire to show liberty is here the motive of our actions. And it seems certain that, however we may imagine we feel a liberty within ourselves, a spectator can commonly infer our actions from our motives and character; and even where he cannot, he concludes in general that he might, were he perfectly acquainted with every circumstance of our situation and temper, and the most secret springs of our complexion and disposition. Now this is the very essence of necessity, according to the foregoing doctrine.

11.23.oldText: 73. But to proceed in this reconciling project with regard to the question of liberty and necessity — the most contentious question of metaphysics, the most contentious science — it will not require many words to prove that all mankind have always agreed in the doctrine of liberty as well as in that of necessity, and that the whole dispute, in this respect too, has so far been merely verbal. For what is meant by liberty when applied to voluntary actions? We cannot surely mean that actions have so little connection with motives, inclinations, and circumstances, that one does not follow from the other with a certain degree of uniformity, and that one affords no inference by which we can conclude the existence of the other. For these are plain and acknowledged matters of fact. By liberty, then, we can only mean _a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will_; that is, if we choose to remain at rest, we may; if we choose to move, we also may. Now this hypothetical liberty is universally allowed to belong to everyone who is not a prisoner and in chains. Here, then, is no subject of dispute.

11.24.oldText: 74. Whatever definition we may give of liberty, we should be careful to observe two necessary circumstances: _first_, that it be consistent with plain matter of fact; _secondly_, that it be consistent with itself. If we observe these circumstances, and make our definition intelligible, I am persuaded that all mankind will be found of one opinion about it.

11.25.oldText: It is universally granted that nothing exists without a cause of its existence, and that chance, when strictly examined, is a mere negative word, meaning no real power that has any being in nature. But it is claimed that some causes are necessary and some not necessary. Here, then, is the advantage of definitions. Let anyone _define_ a cause without including, as part of the definition, a _necessary connection_ with its effect; and let him distinctly show the origin of the idea expressed by the definition; and I shall readily give up the whole controversy. But if the foregoing explication of the matter is accepted, this must be absolutely impracticable. Had objects no regular conjunction with each other, we should never have formed any notion of cause and effect; and this regular conjunction produces that inference of the understanding which is the only connection we can have any comprehension of. Whoever attempts a definition of cause that leaves out these circumstances will be obliged either to use unintelligible terms or such as are synonymous with the term he is trying to define.[18] And if the above definition is admitted, liberty, when opposed to necessity (not to constraint), is the same thing as chance, which is universally allowed to have no existence.

11.26.oldText: [18] Thus, if a cause is defined as _that which produces anything_, it is easy to observe that _producing_ is synonymous with _causing_. In the same way, if a cause is defined as _that by which any thing exists_, this is liable to the same objection. For what is meant by these words, _by which_? Had it been said that a cause is _that_ after which _anything constantly exists_, we should have understood the terms. For this is, indeed, all we know of the matter. And this constancy forms the very essence of necessity, nor have we any other idea of it.

12.0.oldText: 75. There is no method of reasoning more common, and yet none more blameworthy, than, in philosophical disputes, attempting to refute any hypothesis by claiming its dangerous consequences for religion and morality. When any opinion leads to absurdities, it is certainly false; but it is not certain that an opinion is false because it has dangerous consequences. Such tactics, therefore, ought to be avoided entirely, since they contribute nothing to the discovery of truth, but only make the person of an opponent odious. I make this observation in general, without claiming to draw any advantage from it. I frankly submit to an examination of this kind, and shall venture to affirm that the doctrines both of necessity and of liberty, as explained above, are not only consistent with morality, but are absolutely essential to its support.

12.1.oldText: Necessity may be defined in two ways, in line with the two definitions of _cause_, of which it forms an essential part. It consists either in the constant conjunction of like objects, or in the inference of the understanding from one object to another. Now necessity, in both these senses (which are, indeed, fundamentally the same) has universally, though tacitly, in the schools, in the pulpit, and in common life, been allowed to belong to the will of man; and no one has ever pretended to deny that we can draw inferences about human actions, and that those inferences are founded on the experienced union of like actions with like motives, inclinations, and circumstances. The only point on which anyone can differ is, perhaps, that he may refuse to give the name of necessity to this property of human actions; but as long as the meaning is understood, the word can do no harm, I hope. Or he may maintain that it is possible to discover something further in the operations of matter. But this, it must be admitted, can be of no consequence to morality or religion, whatever it may be to natural philosophy or metaphysics. We may here be mistaken in asserting that there is no idea of any other necessity or connection in the actions of body; but surely we ascribe nothing to the actions of the mind beyond what everyone does, and must readily allow. We change no circumstance in the received orthodox system with regard to the will, but only that concerning material objects and causes. Nothing, therefore, can be more innocent, at least, than this doctrine.

12.2.oldText: 76. Since all laws are founded on rewards and punishments, it is supposed as a fundamental principle that these motives have a regular and uniform influence on the mind, both producing good actions and preventing evil ones. We may give to this influence whatever name we please; but, since it is usually conjoined with the action, it must be considered a _cause_, and looked upon as an instance of that necessity which we are seeking to establish here.

12.3.oldText: The only proper object of hatred or vengeance is a person or creature endowed with thought and consciousness; and when any criminal or harmful actions excite that passion, it is only through their relation to the person, or their connection with him. Actions are, by their very nature, temporary and perishing; and where they do not proceed from some _cause_ in the character and disposition of the person who performed them, they can bring him neither honor, if good, nor infamy, if evil. The actions themselves may be blameworthy; they may be contrary to all the rules of morality and religion. But the person is not answerable for them; and since they proceeded from nothing in him that is durable and constant, and leave nothing of that nature behind them, it is impossible that he can, on their account, become the object of punishment or vengeance. According to the principle, therefore, that denies necessity, and consequently causes, a man is as pure and untainted, after committing the most horrid crime, as at the first moment of his birth; nor is his character in any way concerned in his actions, since they do not derive from it, and the wickedness of the one can never be used as proof of the depravity of the other.

12.4.oldText: Men are not blamed for actions they perform ignorantly and accidentally, whatever the consequences may be. Why? Because the principles of these actions are only momentary, and end with them alone. Men are less blamed for actions performed hastily and unpremeditatedly than for those that proceed from deliberation. For what reason? Because a hasty temper, though a constant cause or principle in the mind, operates only by intervals, and does not infect the whole character. Again, repentance wipes away every crime, if accompanied by a reformation of life and manners. How is this to be accounted for? Only by asserting that actions render a person criminal merely insofar as they are proofs of criminal principles in the mind; and when, by an alteration of these principles, they cease to be sound proofs, they likewise cease to be criminal. But, except on the doctrine of necessity, they never were sound proofs, and consequently never were criminal.

12.5.oldText: 77. It will be equally easy to prove, and from the same arguments, that _liberty_, according to the definition mentioned above on which all men agree, is also essential to morality, and that no human actions in which it is lacking are susceptible of any moral qualities, or can be the objects either of approval or disapproval. For since actions are objects of our moral sentiment only insofar as they are indications of internal character, passions, and affections, it is impossible that they can give rise either to praise or blame where they proceed not from these principles, but are derived altogether from external violence.

12.6.oldText: 78. I do not pretend to have obviated or removed all objections to this theory with regard to necessity and liberty. I can foresee other objections, drawn from topics that have not been treated here. It may be said, for instance, that if voluntary actions are subject to the same laws of necessity as the operations of matter, there is a continued chain of necessary causes, pre-ordained and pre-determined, reaching from the original cause of all to every single volition of every human creature. No contingency anywhere in the universe; no indifference; no liberty. While we act, we are at the same time acted upon. The ultimate Author of all our volitions is the Creator of the world, who first bestowed motion on this immense machine, and placed all beings in that particular position from which every subsequent event must, by an inevitable necessity, result. Human actions, therefore, either can have no moral turpitude at all, as proceeding from so good a cause; or, if they have any turpitude, they must involve our Creator in the same guilt, since he is acknowledged to be their ultimate cause and author. For just as a man who sets off a mine is answerable for all the consequences, whether the train he used is long or short, so wherever a continued chain of necessary causes is fixed, that Being — whether finite or infinite — who produces the first, is likewise the author of all the rest, and must bear both the blame and the praise that belong to them. Our clear and unalterable ideas of morality establish this rule, on unquestionable grounds, when we examine the consequences of any human action; and these reasons must have still greater force when applied to the volitions and intentions of a Being infinitely wise and powerful. Ignorance or impotence may be pleaded for so limited a creature as man; but those imperfections have no place in our Creator. He foresaw, he ordained, he intended all those actions of men which we so rashly pronounce criminal. We must therefore conclude either that they are not criminal, or that the Deity, not man, is accountable for them. But since either of these positions is absurd and impious, it follows that the doctrine from which they are deduced cannot possibly be true, as being liable to all the same objections. An absurd consequence, if necessary, proves the original doctrine to be absurd, just as criminal actions render criminal the original cause, if the connection between them is necessary and unavoidable.

12.7.oldText: This objection consists of two parts, which we shall examine separately. _First_, that if human actions can be traced up, by a necessary chain, to the Deity, they can never be criminal, on account of the infinite perfection of that Being from whom they are derived, and who can intend nothing but what is altogether good and praiseworthy. Or, _secondly_, if they are criminal, we must retract the attribute of perfection that we ascribe to the Deity, and must acknowledge him to be the ultimate author of guilt and moral turpitude in all his creatures.

12.8.oldText: 79. The answer to the first objection seems obvious and convincing. There are many philosophers who, after an exact scrutiny of all the phenomena of nature, conclude that the WHOLE, considered as one system, is in every period of its existence ordered with perfect benevolence, and that the utmost possible happiness will, in the end, result to all created beings, without any admixture of positive or absolute ill or misery. Every physical ill, they say, makes an essential part of this benevolent system, and could not possibly be removed, even by the Deity himself, considered as a wise agent, without giving entrance to greater ill, or excluding greater good, which will result from it. From this theory some philosophers, and the ancient _Stoics_ among the rest, drew a topic of consolation under all afflictions, while they taught their pupils that those ills under which they labored were, in reality, goods to the universe, and that to an enlarged view that could comprehend the whole system of nature, every event became an object of joy and exultation. But though this topic is specious and sublime, it was soon found in practice weak and ineffectual. You would surely more irritate than appease a man suffering the racking pains of gout by preaching to him about the rectitude of those general laws that produced the malignant humors in his body, and led them through the proper canals to the sinews and nerves where they now excite such acute torments. These enlarged views may for a moment please the imagination of a speculative man placed in ease and security; but neither can they dwell constantly in his mind, even when undisturbed by the emotions of pain or passion, much less can they maintain their ground when attacked by such powerful antagonists. The affections take a narrower and more natural survey of their object, and by an economy more suited to the infirmity of human minds regard only the beings around us, and are moved by such events as appear good or ill to the private system.

12.9.oldText: 80. The case is the same with _moral_ ill as with _physical_ ill. It cannot reasonably be supposed that those remote considerations, which are found of so little efficacy in the one, will have a more powerful influence in the other. The mind of man is so formed by nature that, on the appearance of certain characters, dispositions, and actions, it immediately feels the sentiment of approval or blame; nor are there any emotions more essential to its frame and constitution. The characters that engage our approval are chiefly those that contribute to the peace and security of human society; the characters that excite blame are chiefly those that tend to public detriment and disturbance. From this it may reasonably be presumed that moral sentiments arise, either mediately or immediately, from a reflection of these opposite interests. What though philosophical meditations establish a different opinion or conjecture — that everything is right with regard to the WHOLE, and that the qualities which disturb society are, on the whole, as beneficial, and as suitable to the primary intention of nature, as those which more directly promote its happiness and welfare? Are such remote and uncertain speculations able to counterbalance the sentiments arising from the natural and immediate view of the objects? A man who is robbed of a considerable sum — does he find his vexation for the loss in any way lessened by these sublime reflections? Why then should his moral resentment against the crime be supposed incompatible with them? Or why should not the acknowledgment of a real distinction between vice and virtue be reconcilable with all speculative systems of philosophy, as well as that of a real distinction between personal beauty and deformity? Both these distinctions are founded in the natural sentiments of the human mind; and these sentiments are not to be controlled or altered by any philosophical theory or speculation whatsoever.

12.10.oldText: 81. The _second_ objection does not admit of so easy and satisfactory an answer; nor is it possible to explain distinctly how the Deity can be the mediate cause of all the actions of men without being the author of sin and moral turpitude. These are mysteries that mere natural and unassisted reason is very unfit to handle; and whatever system she embraces, she must find herself involved in inextricable difficulties, and even contradictions, at every step she takes with regard to such subjects. To reconcile the indifference and contingency of human actions with prescience, or to defend absolute decrees and yet free the Deity from being the author of sin, has been found so far to exceed all the power of philosophy. Happy, if she is thereby made sensible of her temerity when she pries into these sublime mysteries; and, leaving a scene so full of obscurities and perplexities, returns, with suitable modesty, to her true and proper province, the examination of common life — where she will find difficulties enough to employ her inquiries, without launching into so boundless an ocean of doubt, uncertainty, and contradiction!

13.0.oldText: 82. All our reasonings concerning matters of fact are founded on a species of analogy, which leads us to expect from any cause the same events that we have observed to result from similar causes. Where the causes are entirely similar, the analogy is perfect, and the inference drawn from it is regarded as certain and conclusive: nor does any man ever entertain a doubt, when he sees a piece of iron, that it will have weight and cohesion of parts, as in all other instances that have ever fallen under his observation. But where the objects do not have so exact a similarity, the analogy is less perfect, and the inference is less conclusive — though it still has some force, in proportion to the degree of similarity and resemblance. The anatomical observations formed on one animal are, by this kind of reasoning, extended to all animals; and it is certain that when the circulation of the blood, for instance, is clearly proved to take place in one creature, such as a frog or a fish, it forms a strong presumption that the same principle takes place in all. These analogical observations may be carried further, even to this science we are now treating; and any theory by which we explain the operations of the understanding, or the origin and connection of the passions in man, will gain additional authority if we find that the same theory is required to explain the same phenomena in all other animals. We shall test this with regard to the hypothesis by which we have, in the foregoing discourse, tried to account for all experimental reasonings; and it is hoped that this new point of view will serve to confirm all our previous observations.

13.1.oldText: 83. _First_, it seems evident that animals as well as men learn many things from experience, and infer that the same events will always follow from the same causes. By this principle they become acquainted with the more obvious properties of external objects, and gradually, from their birth, store up knowledge of the nature of fire, water, earth, stones, heights, depths, etc., and of the effects that result from their operation. The ignorance and inexperience of the young are here plainly distinguishable from the cunning and sagacity of the old, who have learned, by long observation, to avoid what hurts them and to pursue what gives them ease or pleasure. A horse accustomed to the field becomes acquainted with the proper height he can leap, and will never attempt what exceeds his strength and ability. An old greyhound will leave the more fatiguing part of the chase to the younger, and will place himself so as to meet the hare in her doubles; nor are the conjectures he forms on this occasion founded on anything but his observation and experience.

13.2.oldText: This is still more evident from the effects of discipline and education on animals, who, by the proper application of rewards and punishments, can be taught any course of action, even one most contrary to their natural instincts and propensities. Is it not experience that makes a dog apprehensive of pain when you menace him, or lift up the whip to beat him? Is it not even experience that makes him answer to his name, and infer, from such an arbitrary sound, that you mean him rather than any of his fellows, and intend to call him when you pronounce it in a certain manner, and with a certain tone and accent?

13.3.oldText: In all these cases, we may observe that the animal infers some fact beyond what immediately strikes his senses, and that this inference is altogether founded on past experience, since the creature expects from the present object the same consequences it has always found, in its observation, to result from similar objects.

13.4.oldText: 84. _Secondly_, it is impossible that this inference of the animal can be founded on any process of argument or reasoning, by which it concludes that like events must follow like objects, and that the course of nature will always be regular in its operations. For if there are in reality any arguments of this nature, they surely lie too abstruse for the observation of such imperfect understandings, since it may well employ the utmost care and attention of a philosophic genius to discover and observe them. Animals, therefore, are not guided in these inferences by reasoning; neither are children; neither are the generality of mankind in their ordinary actions and conclusions; neither are philosophers themselves, who, in all the active parts of life, are in the main the same as the common people and are governed by the same maxims. Nature must have provided some other principle, of more ready and more general use and application; nor can an operation of such immense consequence in life as that of inferring effects from causes be trusted to the uncertain process of reasoning and argumentation. Were this doubtful with regard to men, it seems to admit of no question with regard to the brute creation; and once the conclusion is firmly established in the one case, we have a strong presumption, from all the rules of analogy, that it ought to be universally admitted, without exception or reservation. It is custom alone that leads animals, from every object that strikes their senses, to infer its usual attendant, and carries their imagination, from the appearance of the one, to conceive the other in that particular manner we call _belief_. No other explication can be given of this operation in all the higher, as well as the lower, classes of sensitive beings that fall under our notice and observation.[19]

13.5.oldText: [19] Since all reasoning concerning facts or causes derives merely from custom, it may be asked how it happens that men so much surpass animals in reasoning, and one man so much surpasses another. Does not the same custom have the same influence on all?

13.6.oldText: We shall here try briefly to explain the great difference in human understandings; after which the reason for the difference between men and animals will easily be grasped.

13.7.oldText: 1. When we have lived some time, and have become used to the uniformity of nature, we acquire a general habit by which we always transfer the known to the unknown, and conceive the latter to resemble the former. By means of this general habitual principle, we regard even a single experiment as the foundation of reasoning, and expect a similar event with some degree of certainty, where the experiment has been made accurately and free from all foreign circumstances. It is therefore considered as a matter of great importance to observe the consequences of things; and since one man may very much surpass another in attention, memory, and observation, this will make a very great difference in their reasoning.

13.8.oldText: 2. Where there is a complication of causes to produce any effect, one mind may be much larger than another, and better able to grasp the whole system of objects and to infer their consequences soundly.

13.9.oldText: 3. One man is able to carry on a chain of consequences to a greater length than another.

13.10.oldText: 4. Few men can think for long without running into a confusion of ideas, and mistaking one for another; and there are various degrees of this infirmity.

13.11.oldText: 5. The circumstance on which the effect depends is frequently involved in other circumstances that are foreign and extrinsic. To separate it often requires great attention, accuracy, and subtlety.

13.12.oldText: 6. The forming of general maxims from particular observations is a very delicate operation; and nothing is more common, from haste or a narrowness of mind that does not see on all sides, than to make mistakes on this point.

13.13.oldText: 7. When we reason from analogies, the man who has the greater experience, or the greater quickness in suggesting analogies, will be the better reasoner.

13.14.oldText: 8. Biases from prejudice, education, passion, party, etc., weigh more on one mind than on another.

13.15.oldText: 9. After we have gained confidence in human testimony, books and conversation enlarge the sphere of one man's experience and thought much more than those of another.

13.16.oldText: It would be easy to discover many other circumstances that make a difference in the understandings of men.

13.17.oldText: 85. But though animals learn many parts of their knowledge from observation, there are also many parts that they derive from the original hand of nature, which much exceed the share of capacity they possess on ordinary occasions, and in which they improve little or nothing by the longest practice and experience. These we call Instincts, and are so apt to admire as something very extraordinary, and inexplicable by all the disquisitions of human understanding. But our wonder will perhaps cease or diminish when we consider that the experimental reasoning itself, which we possess in common with beasts, and on which the whole conduct of life depends, is nothing but a species of instinct or mechanical power that acts in us unknown to ourselves, and in its chief operations is not directed by any such relations or comparisons of ideas as are the proper objects of our intellectual faculties. Though the instinct is different, it is still an instinct that teaches a man to avoid the fire — just as much as that which teaches a bird, with such exactness, the art of incubation, and the whole economy and order of its nursery.

14.0.oldText: 86. In Dr. Tillotson's writings there is an argument against the _real presence_ as concise, elegant, and strong as any argument can possibly be supposed against a doctrine so little worthy of serious refutation. It is acknowledged on all hands, says that learned prelate, that the authority of either scripture or tradition is founded merely on the testimony of the apostles, who were eyewitnesses to those miracles of our Savior by which he proved his divine mission. Our evidence, then, for the truth of the Christian religion is less than the evidence for the truth of our senses; because, even in the first authors of our religion, it was no greater; and it is evident it must diminish in passing from them to their disciples; nor can anyone rest such confidence in their testimony as in the immediate object of his senses. But a weaker evidence can never destroy a stronger; and therefore, even were the doctrine of the real presence ever so clearly revealed in scripture, it would be directly contrary to the rules of sound reasoning to give our assent to it. It contradicts sense, though both scripture and tradition, on which it is supposed to be built, do not carry such evidence with them as sense, when they are considered merely as external evidences, and are not brought home to every one's breast by the immediate operation of the Holy Spirit.

14.1.oldText: Nothing is so convenient as a decisive argument of this kind, which must at least _silence_ the most arrogant bigotry and superstition, and free us from their impertinent solicitations. I flatter myself that I have discovered an argument of a similar nature which, if sound, will, with the wise and learned, be an everlasting check on all kinds of superstitious delusion, and consequently will be useful as long as the world endures. For that long, I presume, accounts of miracles and prodigies will be found in all history, sacred and profane.

14.2.oldText: 87. Though experience is our only guide in reasoning concerning matters of fact, it must be admitted that this guide is not entirely infallible, but in some cases is apt to lead us into errors. Someone who, in our climate, should expect better weather in any week of June than in one of December, would reason soundly and in accordance with experience; but it is certain that he may, in the event, find himself mistaken. We may observe, however, that in such a case he would have no cause to complain of experience, because it commonly informs us beforehand of the uncertainty, by that contrariety of events which we may learn from diligent observation. Not all effects follow with the same certainty from their supposed causes. Some events are found, in all countries and ages, to have been constantly conjoined together; others are found to have been more variable, and sometimes to disappoint our expectations; so that in our reasonings about matters of fact there are all imaginable degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty to the lowest species of moral evidence.

14.3.oldText: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence. In conclusions founded on infallible experience, he expects the event with the last degree of assurance, and regards his past experience as a full _proof_ of the future existence of that event. In other cases he proceeds more cautiously: he weighs the opposing experiments; he considers which side is supported by the greater number of experiments; to that side he inclines, with doubt and hesitation; and when he at last fixes his judgment, the evidence does not exceed what we properly call _probability_. All probability, then, supposes an opposition of experiments and observations, where the one side is found to outweigh the other, and to produce a degree of evidence proportioned to the superiority. A hundred instances or experiments on one side, and fifty on another, afford a doubtful expectation of any event; while a hundred uniform experiments, with only one that is contradictory, reasonably give rise to a fairly strong degree of assurance. In all cases we must balance the opposing experiments, where they are opposing, and subtract the smaller number from the greater, in order to know the exact force of the superior evidence.

14.4.oldText: 88. To apply these principles to a particular instance: we may observe that there is no kind of reasoning more common, more useful, and even necessary to human life, than that derived from the testimony of men and the reports of eyewitnesses and spectators. This kind of reasoning, one may perhaps deny to be founded on the relation of cause and effect. I shall not dispute about a word. It is enough to observe that our assurance in any argument of this kind is derived from no other principle than our observation of the truthfulness of human testimony, and of the usual conformity of facts to the reports of witnesses. Since it is a general maxim that no objects have any discoverable connection together, and that all the inferences we can draw from one to another are founded merely on our experience of their constant and regular conjunction, it is evident that we ought not to make an exception to this maxim in favor of human testimony, whose connection with any event seems, in itself, as little necessary as any other. Were not memory tenacious to a certain degree; had not men commonly an inclination to truth and a principle of integrity; were they not sensible to shame when detected in a falsehood — were not these qualities, I say, discovered by experience to be inherent in human nature, we should never repose the least confidence in human testimony. A man who is delirious, or noted for falsehood and villainy, has no manner of authority with us.

14.5.oldText: And since the evidence derived from witnesses and human testimony is founded on past experience, it varies with experience, and is regarded either as a _proof_ or as a _probability_, according as the conjunction between any particular kind of report and any kind of object has been found to be constant or variable. There are a number of circumstances to be taken into consideration in all judgments of this kind; and the ultimate standard by which we settle all disputes that may arise concerning them is always derived from experience and observation. Where this experience is not entirely uniform on either side, it is attended by an unavoidable contrariety in our judgments, and by the same opposition and mutual destruction of argument as in every other kind of evidence. We frequently hesitate about the reports of others. We balance the opposing circumstances that cause any doubt or uncertainty; and when we discover a superiority on any side, we incline toward it, but still with a diminution of assurance, in proportion to the force of its antagonist.

14.6.oldText: 89. This contrariety of evidence, in the present case, may arise from several different causes: from the opposition of contrary testimony; from the character or number of the witnesses; from the manner of their delivering their testimony; or from the union of all these circumstances. We entertain a suspicion about any matter of fact when the witnesses contradict each other; when they are few in number, or of doubtful character; when they have an interest in what they affirm; when they deliver their testimony with hesitation, or, on the contrary, with too violent assertions. There are many other particulars of the same kind that may diminish or destroy the force of any argument derived from human testimony.

14.7.oldText: Suppose, for instance, that the fact which the testimony tries to establish partakes of the extraordinary and the marvelous; in that case, the evidence resulting from the testimony admits of a diminution, greater or less, in proportion as the fact is more or less unusual. The reason why we place any credit in witnesses and historians is not derived from any _connection_ we perceive _a priori_ between testimony and reality, but because we are accustomed to find a conformity between them. But when the fact attested is one that has seldom fallen under our observation, here is a contest of two opposite experiences, of which the one destroys the other, as far as its force goes, and the superior can only operate on the mind by the force that remains. The very same principle of experience that gives us a certain degree of assurance in the testimony of witnesses also gives us, in this case, another degree of assurance against the fact they try to establish; from which contradiction there necessarily arises a counterpoise, and mutual destruction of belief and authority.

14.8.oldText: _I should not believe such a story were it told me by Cato_, was a proverbial saying in Rome, even during the lifetime of that philosophical patriot.[20] The incredibility of a fact, it was allowed, might invalidate even so great an authority.

14.10.oldText: The Indian prince who refused to believe the first reports about the effects of frost reasoned soundly; and it naturally required very strong testimony to win his assent to facts that arose from a state of nature with which he was unacquainted, and which bore so little analogy to those events of which he had had constant and uniform experience. Though they were not contrary to his experience, they were not conformable to it.[21]

14.11.oldText: [21] No Indian, it is evident, could have experience that water did not freeze in cold climates. This is placing nature in a situation quite unknown to him; and it is impossible for him to tell _a priori_ what will result from it. It is making a new experiment, the outcome of which is always uncertain. One may sometimes conjecture from analogy what will follow; but still this is only conjecture. And it must be admitted that, in the present case of freezing, the event follows contrary to the rules of analogy, and is such as a rational Indian would not look for. The operations of cold upon water are not gradual, according to the degrees of cold; but whenever it reaches the freezing point, the water passes in a moment, from the utmost fluidity to perfect hardness. Such an event, therefore, may be called _extraordinary_, and requires fairly strong testimony to make it credible to people in a warm climate. But still it is not _miraculous_, nor contrary to uniform experience of the course of nature in cases where all the circumstances are the same. The inhabitants of Sumatra have always seen water fluid in their own climate, and the freezing of their rivers ought to be considered a prodigy; but they have never seen water in Muscovy during the winter, and therefore they cannot reasonably be positive about what would there be the consequence.

14.12.oldText: 90.
